title: Sparks of Cooperative Reasoning: LLMs as Strategic Hanabi Agents
claim: A minimal prompt with only explicit state is contrasted with a scaffolded prompt that adds derived belief-state deductions and structured reasoning.
layout: 3 regions: game state left, two stacked prompt routes feeding one LLM, color-coded
description: A large yellow 'Game State' panel on the left holds the Hanabi state. Its shared part shows firework cards, life and info tokens, and a discard pile. Its private part shows the agent's partially known hand and the partner's fully visible hand. Two routes lead from it to a robot icon labeled LLM, and from the robot to an orange 'Action' box. The top route, in a light-blue 'Watson' box, goes through a 'Prompt Summary' that lists the state, lists legal moves, and gives a simple instruction. The bottom route, in a pink 'Sherlock' box, adds a green 'Deductive Context' block of card possibilities through a '+' sign. It also has a second 'Prompt Summary' with step-by-step probabilistic reasoning, whose orange arrow goes up into the LLM. Blue arrows mark the Watson route and orange arrows mark the Sherlock route.
caption: \normalsize A comparison of the \basic: provides basic game state with only explicit knowledge and \best settings, which scaffolds the agent by providing belief state: listing all valid color/rank possibilities for every card in a "Deductive Context" block and enforcing a step-by-step Bayesian reasoning process for a 2-player Hanabi game.
abstract: Cooperative reasoning under incomplete information remains challenging for both humans and multi-agent systems. The card game Hanabi embodies this challenge, requiring theory-of-mind reasoning and strategic communication. We benchmark 17 state-of-the-art LLM agents in 2-5 player games and study the impact of context engineering across model scales (4B to 600B+) to understand persistent coordination failures and robustness to scaffolding: from a minimal prompt with only explicit card details (Watson setting), to scaffolding with programmatic, Bayesian-motivated deductions (Sherlock), to multi-turn state tracking via working memory (Mycroft setting). We show that (1) agents can maintain an internal working memory for state tracking and (2) cross-play performance between different LLMs smoothly interpolates with model strength. In the Sherlock setting, the strongest reasoning models exceed 15 points on average across player counts, yet still trail experienced humans and specialist Hanabi agents, both consistently scoring above 20. We release the first public Hanabi datasets with annotated trajectories and move utilities: (1) HanabiLogs, containing 1,520 full game logs for instruction tuning, and (2) HanabiRewards, containing 560 games with dense move-level value annotations for all candidate moves. Supervised and RL finetuning of a 4B open-weight model (Qwen3-Instruct) on our datasets improves cooperative Hanabi play by 21% and 156% respectively, bringing performance to within ~3 points of a strong proprietary reasoning model (o4-mini) and surpassing the best non-reasoning model (GPT-4.1) by 52%. The HanabiRewards RL-finetuned model further generalizes beyond Hanabi, improving performance on a cooperative group-guessing benchmark by 11%, temporal reasoning on EventQA by 6.4 points, instruction-following on IFBench by 1.7 Pass@10, and matching AIME 2025 mathematical reasoning Pass@10.
